name: Francisco Fernández Ochoa
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in slalom at the 1972 Winter Olympics in Sapporo at age 21, becoming Spain's first-ever Winter Olympic gold medalist and first Spanish Olympic champion since 1928.
early_history_summary: Born in Madrid and raised in Cercedilla near the Navacerrada ski resort, Fernández Ochoa was the eldest of eight children whose father ran a local ski school. He learned to ski there alongside his siblings and made his Olympic debut at age 17 at the 1968 Grenoble Games. He made his World Cup debut in January 1969 and had several top-ten finishes before his stunning Olympic gold in 1972.
family_context_summary: Eldest of eight children; father ran a local ski school in Cercedilla near the Navacerrada ski resort, providing direct domain immersion from childhood. Four of his siblings also became Olympic alpine skiers.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father operated a ski school, giving Francisco direct access to skiing instruction, equipment, and terrain from an early age. The family was deeply embedded in the sport, with five children competing at the Olympic level.
primary_early_advantage_tags: ski school father, sibling skiers, early terrain access, Olympic debut at 17
evidence_summary: Francisco Fernández Ochoa grew up in a ski-family ecosystem: his father ran a ski school in Cercedilla, and five of eight children became Olympic alpine skiers. He had direct domain immersion from childhood, made his Olympic debut at 17, and won a stunning slalom gold at the 1972 Sapporo Olympics at age 21 — Spain's first Winter Olympic gold medalist ever. His victory was a major upset; he had never won an international meet before. The family-domain apprenticeship was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Madrid in 1950, the eldest of eight children; father ran a local ski school in Cercedilla near the Navacerrada ski resort, providing a modest but sport-immersed family environment.
current_position: Died on 6 November 2006 at age 56 in Cercedilla, Spain, from lymphatic cancer; final status: Spain's only Winter Olympic gold medalist, with a statue erected in his hometown shortly before his death.

trajectory.event: Made Olympic debut at the Grenoble Winter Olympics, finishing 38th in downhill, 38th in giant slalom, and 23rd in slalom.
Made FIS World Cup debut in January 1969, recording his first top-ten finish (sixth in slalom at Megève).
Won Olympic gold medal in slalom at the Sapporo Winter Olympics, becoming Spain's first Winter Olympic champion and first Olympic champion in any sport since 1928.
Won his only World Cup slalom victory at Zakopane, Poland, and earned a bronze medal in the slalom at the World Championships — Spain's first-ever World Championship skiing medal.
Competed at the Innsbruck Winter Olympics, his third of four Olympic appearances.
Retired from competitive skiing after the Lake Placid Winter Olympics, his fourth Olympic Games.
Died of lymphatic cancer on 6 November 2006 in Cercedilla, barely a week after a statue honoring him was unveiled in his hometown.

name: Kalinikos Kreanga
milestone_by_age_26: Won a European Championships bronze medal in mixed doubles at the 1988 Paris event representing Romania at age 16, followed by a World Championships bronze in mixed doubles (1991) and two European Championship golds (1992, 1994) — all before age 26.
early_history_summary: Born as Călin Creangă in Bistrița, Romania, Kreanga started playing table tennis at age 7 under coach Gheorghe Bozga. At 17, he defected from Communist Romania while at the 1989 European Youth Championships in Luxembourg, moved to Greece, acquired citizenship, and changed his name to Kalinikos Kreanga. He quickly became one of Europe's dominant table tennis players in the early 1990s.
family_context_summary: Born in Bistrița, Romania; defected with his father at age 17 in 1989. Family background details beyond this are not well documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father accompanied him during his defection, suggesting family support for his table tennis career, but no specific domain expertise is documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early start at 7, dedicated coach, defection catalyst, youth championships
evidence_summary: Kreanga started table tennis at age 7 under coach Gheorghe Bozga in Romania, giving him a decade of serious reps before his first international medal at 16. His defection at 17 from Communist Romania was a constraint-driven catalyst that led to Greek citizenship and a new competitive ecosystem. By 26, he had won European Championship golds (1992, 1994), a World Championship bronze (1991), and multiple other European medals. His backhand topspin is regarded as one of the most devastating in table tennis history.
starting_point: Born as Călin Creangă in 1972 in Bistrița, Romania; started playing table tennis at age 7 under a local coach, in a Communist-era Romanian sports system.
current_position: Retired from professional table tennis; regarded as one of the dominant European players of the 1990s-2000s, reaching a career-high world ranking of No. 7 in 2004; living in Greece.

name: Ana Ivanovic
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2008 French Open (Grand Slam) at age 20 and became WTA world No. 1; also won first WTA title at Canberra in 2005 at age 17 and reached the 2007 French Open final at age 19.
early_history_summary: Born in Belgrade, SFR Yugoslavia, Ivanovic started playing tennis at age 5 after watching Monica Seles on television. She practiced on a makeshift court in an empty swimming pool during the NATO bombing of Belgrade in 1999. She turned pro in August 2003, won five ITF titles in 2004, and broke into the WTA top 100. By 2005 she won her first WTA title and reached the top 20. She won the 2008 French Open at age 20, becoming world No. 1.
family_context_summary: Mother Dragana is a lawyer; father Miroslav is a self-employed businessman; younger brother Miloš. The family was middle-class in Belgrade but none played tennis before Ana. The family endured the NATO bombing of Belgrade in 1999.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family tennis background; Ana discovered tennis independently by watching Monica Seles on TV and memorizing a tennis school phone number. Parents supported her but had no domain expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: war-era practice, early start at 5, NATO bombing adversity, self-driven
evidence_summary: Ana Ivanovic began tennis at age 5 in Belgrade, self-motivated after watching Monica Seles on TV. Her family had no tennis background — her mother was a lawyer and father a businessman. She practiced in an empty swimming pool during the NATO bombing of 1999, a significant adversity constraint. She turned pro at 15, won her first WTA title at 17, and claimed the 2008 French Open at 20 to become world No. 1. Her early path was defined by self-driven repetition in difficult circumstances rather than inherited advantages.
starting_point: Born in 1987 in Belgrade, SFR Yugoslavia to a middle-class family; mother a lawyer, father a self-employed businessman, no tennis background in the family.
current_position: Retired from professional tennis in December 2016; married German footballer Bastian Schweinsteiger; former world No. 1 and 2008 French Open champion; resides in Switzerland.

Won the French Open Grand Slam title and became WTA world No. 1 for the first time.
Won the year-end WTA Tournament of Champions and began a career resurgence after dropping to No. 65 in the rankings.
Returned to the top of the game, winning four WTA titles and finishing the year as world No. 5.
Announced retirement from professional tennis in December 2016.

name: Assar Rönnlund
milestone_by_age_26: Won two gold medals (15 km and 4×10 km relay) and a silver (50 km) at the 1962 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships in Zakopane at age 26, earning the Svenska Dagbladet Gold Medal as Sweden's best sports feat of the year.
early_history_summary: Born in Sävar near Umeå, Sweden, Rönnlund grew up in the small village of Ytterträsk. His father was a lumberjack, and at 15 Assar worked in the forest as a timberman. He broke through at the 1959 Swedish Championships, winning gold in the 30 km ahead of favorite Sixten Jernberg. He competed at the 1960 Olympics (12th in 50 km) before his dominant 1962 World Championships performance.
family_context_summary: Father was a lumberjack in the small village of Ytterträsk in Sävar municipality, northern Sweden. Assar worked as a timberman at age 15. The family was working-class in a rural Nordic setting.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental skiing expertise, but growing up in rural northern Sweden provided natural proximity to cross-country skiing culture and terrain.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Nordic skiing culture, rural forest upbringing, IFK Umeå club, early physical labor
evidence_summary: Assar Rönnlund grew up in a small logging village in northern Sweden, the son of a lumberjack, and worked as a timberman at 15. This rural Nordic environment provided deep immersion in cross-country skiing culture and terrain. He broke through at the 1959 Swedish Championships and won two golds and a silver at the 1962 World Championships at age 26, earning Sweden's top sports honor. His path was defined by geographic immersion in a skiing frontier and physical labor from a young age rather than inherited advantages.
starting_point: Born in 1935 in Sävar near Umeå, northern Sweden; son of a lumberjack in the small village of Ytterträsk, working-class rural background.
current_position: Died on 5 January 2011 at age 75 in Umeå, Sweden; final career: Swedish cross-country skiing champion and later radio commentator for Swedish Radio from 1972 to 2003.

name: Mijaín López
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in Greco-Roman wrestling (120 kg) at the 2008 Beijing Olympics at age 25, becoming Olympic champion. He also won gold at the 2003 Pan American Games at age 21 and placed 5th at the 2004 Athens Olympics.
early_history_summary: Born in Entronque de Herradura, Cuba, López began wrestling at age 10 after a local trainer noticed his exceptional strength. He joined the Cuban national team at 17 and trained at Cuba's sports initiation schools (EIDE and ESPA). He won his first major title at the 2003 Pan American Games at 21, competed at the 2004 Olympics (5th place), and won his first Olympic gold at Beijing 2008 at age 25. His brother Michel López won an Olympic bronze in boxing at Athens 2004.
family_context_summary: Born in a small town in Pinar del Río, Cuba; brothers Misael and Michel were also athletes, with Michel winning an Olympic bronze in boxing at Athens 2004. Family worked in agriculture; López built strength carrying fruit crates and chasing animals.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental wrestling expertise, but the family had a strong athletic culture with multiple brothers competing at elite levels in combat sports.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cuban sports school system, national team at 17, exceptional physical size, athletic siblings
evidence_summary: Mijaín López grew up in rural Cuba with exceptional physical stature from childhood, which attracted a local wrestling coach. He entered Cuba's elite sports pipeline (EIDE, ESPA) and joined the senior national team at 17. His brother Michel won Olympic boxing bronze in 2004, indicating a family athletic culture. López won Pan American Games gold at 21 and Olympic gold at 25 in Beijing. The Cuban state sports system provided sustained coaching and competition infrastructure from a young age, complementing his extraordinary physical gifts.
starting_point: Born in 1982 in Entronque de Herradura, a small town in Pinar del Río, Cuba; from a rural agricultural family with strong athletic tradition among brothers.
current_position: Retired from competitive wrestling after the 2024 Paris Olympics; five-time Olympic gold medalist (2008-2024), the first athlete to win five consecutive Olympic golds in the same individual event; widely considered the greatest wrestler of all time.

Won second consecutive Olympic gold medal at the London Olympics.
Won third consecutive Olympic gold at the Rio Olympics in the 130 kg category.
Won fifth consecutive Olympic gold medal at the Paris Olympics, becoming the first athlete ever to achieve this in the same individual event, then retired.

name: Czesława Kwoka
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Kwoka was murdered at Auschwitz on 12 March 1943 at age 14. She never had the opportunity to achieve any milestone. Her posthumous recognition as a symbol of Holocaust victims came decades later through colorized photographs.
early_history_summary: Czesława Kwoka was a Polish Catholic girl born on 15 August 1928 in Wólka Złojecka, Poland. She and her mother Katarzyna were deported from the Zamość region to Auschwitz on 13 December 1942 during Operation Zamość. She was photographed by prisoner Wilhelm Brasse upon arrival, showing a cut lip from being beaten by a guard. She was murdered with a phenol injection to the heart on 12 March 1943 at age 14.
family_context_summary: Born to Katarzyna and Paweł Kwoka in the village of Wólka Złojecka in the Zamość region of Poland. A Polish Catholic farming family deported during Operation Zamość.
evidence_summary: Czesława Kwoka was a 14-year-old Polish Catholic girl murdered at Auschwitz in 1943. She never had the opportunity to achieve any personal milestone. Her posthumous fame as a symbol of Holocaust victims came through colorized registration photographs shared by the Auschwitz-Birkenau Museum decades later. The birth year listed in the source CSV (1943) appears to be her death year; she was actually born in 1928. No material milestone by age 26 was possible.
